title: English Language Assessment · UK
summary: UK workplace English: regional listening, vocabulary, reading, writing and speaking. One randomly selected conversation per attempt.
instructions: Complete four 15-minute sections in order. Each section begins with an instruction screen and presents one task at a time. Audio can be played once. You cannot return to a completed section.
about: A rigorous English communication assessment for roles that require clear, accurate, and confident workplace communication.

task.title: English Language Assessment · UK
task.description: Demonstrate practical command of English through realistic workplace and public-service communication scenarios.
task.instructions: The assessment contains four timed sections. Listening and reading include objective questions. Writing and speaking require original responses and are reviewed for coherence, vocabulary, grammar, fluency, pronunciation, and task fulfilment. Use UK workplace vocabulary and spelling where appropriate; clear communication and intelligibility remain the scoring criteria.

standard.name: Valases Workplace English Framework
standard.disclaimer: The reported CEFR band is an assessment estimate, not an accredited language certificate.

sections.label: Listening
sections.description: Listen to one everyday or workplace conversation and answer questions about detail, purpose and inference.
sections.intro: You will hear one everyday or workplace conversation. The recording plays once. Answer the questions from memory after it finishes.
rules: Audio plays once and cannot be restarted.
Notes on paper are not permitted.

sections.label: Reading
sections.description: Read two professional texts and distinguish central claims, supporting detail, exceptions, and implications.
sections.intro: Each question includes the text you need. Read for meaning rather than matching isolated words. Choose one answer and continue.
rules: One question is shown at a time.
You may reread the passage while answering.

items.label: Policy analysis
items.passage: Remote work requests are reviewed according to business continuity rather than seniority. Employees should submit a request at least five working days in advance and explain how customer coverage, confidential information, and handovers will be managed. A manager may approve a shorter notice period when an unexpected event makes the normal process impractical. Approval is not permanent: arrangements are reviewed every quarter, and an arrangement may be changed if service levels decline or security controls are not followed.
items.prompt: Which principle has the greatest influence on approval?
options: Length of service
Operational continuity
The employee's commute
The permanence of the request

items.label: Policy analysis

Employees should submit a request at least five working days in advance and explain how customer coverage, confidential information, and handovers will be managed. A manager may approve a shorter notice period when an unexpected event makes the normal process impractical. Approval is not permanent: arrangements are reviewed every quarter, and an arrangement may be changed if service levels decline or security controls are not followed.
items.prompt: What does the exception for shorter notice imply?
options: The five-day rule is optional for everyone
Managers can exercise judgement when circumstances are unexpected
Only permanent arrangements need approval
Security controls may be ignored temporarily
items.answer: Managers can exercise judgement when circumstances are unexpected

items.label: Policy consequence
items.passage: Remote work requests are reviewed according to business continuity rather than seniority. Employees should submit a request at least five working days in advance and explain how customer coverage, confidential information, and handovers will be managed. A manager may approve a shorter notice period when an unexpected event makes the normal process impractical. Approval is not permanent: arrangements are reviewed every quarter, and an arrangement may be changed if service levels decline or security controls are not followed.
items.prompt: Which situation most clearly justifies changing an approved arrangement?
options: The employee has completed another quarter
Customer coverage has become unreliable
A more senior employee submits a request
The employee moves closer to the office

items.label: Evidence and inference
items.passage: The pilot reduced the average time required to resolve routine support requests by 18 percent. However, customer satisfaction remained unchanged. Interviews suggested that faster closure did not always mean clearer communication: several customers said they received a solution without understanding why the problem occurred. The operations team therefore recommends extending the pilot only if the next phase measures explanation quality as well as speed.
items.prompt: Why does the team attach a condition to extending the pilot?
options: The speed improvement was too small
The pilot increased operating costs
Efficiency alone did not improve the customer experience
Customers preferred slower service
items.answer: Efficiency alone did not improve the customer experience

items.label: Evidence and inference
items.passage: The pilot reduced the average time required to resolve routine support requests by 18 percent. However, customer satisfaction remained unchanged. Interviews suggested that faster closure did not always mean clearer communication: several customers said they received a solution without understanding why the problem occurred. The operations team therefore recommends extending the pilot only if the next phase measures explanation quality as well as speed.
items.prompt: Which statement best summarises the evidence?
options: Faster resolution guaranteed better service
Customers rejected the solutions they received
The pilot improved speed but exposed a communication gap
The team recommends ending all automation
items.answer: The pilot improved speed but exposed a communication gap

items.label: Recommendation logic
items.passage: The pilot reduced the average time required to resolve routine support requests by 18 percent. However, customer satisfaction remained unchanged. Interviews suggested that faster closure did not always mean clearer communication: several customers said they received a solution without understanding why the problem occurred. The operations team therefore recommends extending the pilot only if the next phase measures explanation quality as well as speed.
items.prompt: Which assumption underpins the recommendation?
options: Resolution speed and explanation quality should be assessed together
Customer interviews are less reliable than closure data
Only automated requests require explanations
Satisfaction will improve automatically in a larger pilot
items.answer: Resolution speed and explanation quality should be assessed together

items.label: Procurement judgement
items.passage: The lowest-priced supplier met the technical specification but proposed an implementation team based entirely outside the customer's operating hours. The second-ranked bid was 7 percent more expensive and included regional support, a named transition manager, and service credits if critical milestones were missed. Procurement may still recommend the lower bid, but the evaluation note must quantify the operational risk and explain why the existing support model is sufficient. Price alone cannot determine the award because continuity during transition is classified as a material requirement.
items.prompt: Why can the lowest price not determine the award by itself?
options: Regional suppliers must always be selected
Transition continuity is a material requirement
Service credits are prohibited
The technical specification has changed
items.answer: Transition continuity is a material requirement

items.label: Procurement judgement
items.passage: The lowest-priced supplier met the technical specification but proposed an implementation team based entirely outside the customer's operating hours. The second-ranked bid was 7 percent more expensive and included regional support, a named transition manager, and service credits if critical milestones were missed. Procurement may still recommend the lower bid, but the evaluation note must quantify the operational risk and explain why the existing support model is sufficient. Price alone cannot determine the award because continuity during transition is classified as a material requirement.
items.prompt: What must procurement demonstrate to recommend the lower bid?
options: That the second supplier withdrew
That the identified operating-hours risk is understood and adequately controlled
That every technical requirement is optional
That service credits have no financial value
items.answer: That the identified operating-hours risk is understood and adequately controlled

items.label: Procurement inference
items.passage: The lowest-priced supplier met the technical specification but proposed an implementation team based entirely outside the customer's operating hours. The second-ranked bid was 7 percent more expensive and included regional support, a named transition manager, and service credits if critical milestones were missed. Procurement may still recommend the lower bid, but the evaluation note must quantify the operational risk and explain why the existing support model is sufficient. Price alone cannot determine the award because continuity during transition is classified as a material requirement.
items.prompt: Which statement best captures the evaluator's required position?
options: Cost should be ignored whenever delivery teams are remote
A compliant bid may still be inferior when implementation risk is considered
The higher bid automatically offers better technical quality
Operational risk can be accepted without written justification
items.answer: A compliant bid may still be inferior when implementation risk is considered

items.label: Incident communication
items.passage: At 09:20 UTC, monitoring detected intermittent delays affecting invoice exports. Core transaction processing remained available, and no evidence of data loss was found. The team disabled a recently introduced queue optimisation at 10:05 UTC, after which export times returned to normal. Investigation continues because the rollback restored performance but did not explain why the change affected only two regions. The next customer update will be issued by 14:00 UTC even if root-cause analysis is still in progress.
items.prompt: What is confirmed about the incident?
options: All transaction processing stopped
The rollback restored export performance
Customer data was permanently lost
The root cause was identified by 10:05 UTC

items.label: Incident communication
items.passage: At 09:20 UTC, monitoring detected intermittent delays affecting invoice exports. Core transaction processing remained available, and no evidence of data loss was found. The team disabled a recently introduced queue optimisation at 10:05 UTC, after which export times returned to normal. Investigation continues because the rollback restored performance but did not explain why the change affected only two regions. The next customer update will be issued by 14:00 UTC even if root-cause analysis is still in progress.
items.prompt: Why does the team continue investigating after performance returns to normal?
options: The mitigation does not explain the regional pattern
Monitoring is no longer available
The rollback caused data loss
Invoice exports remain completely unavailable
items.answer: The mitigation does not explain the regional pattern

items.label: Communication commitment
items.passage: At 09:20 UTC, monitoring detected intermittent delays affecting invoice exports. Core transaction processing remained available, and no evidence of data loss was found. The team disabled a recently introduced queue optimisation at 10:05 UTC, after which export times returned to normal. Investigation continues because the rollback restored performance but did not explain why the change affected only two regions. The next customer update will be issued by 14:00 UTC even if root-cause analysis is still in progress.
items.prompt: What does the final sentence signal to customers?
options: Updates depend on having a complete technical explanation
The team is committing to a communication time independently of investigation completion
No further update will be needed if exports remain stable
Only affected regions will receive information
items.answer: The team is committing to a communication time independently of investigation completion

sections.label: Writing
sections.description: Produce a concise summary and a professional email with clear purpose, structure, and tone.
sections.intro: Complete both writing tasks. Quality, relevance, grammar, vocabulary, organisation, and adherence to the word range are reviewed.
rules: Stay within the displayed word range.
Spend about 5 minutes on Task 1 and 10 minutes on Task 2.

items.label: Executive summary
items.passage: A four-day working week can improve focus when organisations redesign work rather than compressing the same workload into fewer days. Successful trials remove low-value meetings, clarify decision ownership, and protect periods for concentrated work. Where these changes are absent, employees may face longer days and greater pressure, cancelling the intended wellbeing benefit. The strongest evidence therefore supports treating shorter weeks as an operational redesign, not simply a scheduling benefit.
items.prompt: Summarise the central conclusion and its main qualification in one paragraph for a senior manager.

items.label: Customer recovery email
items.prompt: A London customer paid a £250 set-up fee, but a promised implementation update was late and incomplete. Write a customer service email acknowledging the issue, explaining immediate next steps without unsupported promises, and proposing a follow-up time in UK local time. Use UK workplace vocabulary and spelling.

sections.label: Speaking
sections.description: Record four workplace responses that test intelligibility, practical interaction, structured explanation, and extended speaking.
sections.intro: Test your microphone first. Each scored prompt provides brief preparation time followed by one recording attempt.
rules: Use a headset microphone if available.
Speak at a natural pace and volume.
Scored responses cannot be played back or rerecorded.

items.label: Read aloud
items.prompt: Read the text aloud clearly.
items.passage: Effective teams do not avoid disagreement. They make it safe to question assumptions, examine evidence, and decide who is responsible for the next action. When disagreement is handled respectfully, it becomes a tool for better decisions rather than a source of delay.

items.label: Respond to a situation
items.prompt: You are leading a meeting. A colleague repeatedly interrupts another speaker. Address the colleague politely, protect the discussion, and explain how the meeting will continue.

items.label: Explain operational information
items.passage: Support backlog: Monday 84 cases; Tuesday 61; Wednesday 39. First-response target met: Monday 72%; Tuesday 81%; Wednesday 93%.
items.prompt: Brief a manager on the trend, connect the two measures, and identify one sensible follow-up question.

items.label: Extended workplace response
items.prompt: A project is on schedule, but a key dependency has become uncertain. Explain how you would communicate the risk to a senior stakeholder without causing unnecessary alarm. Include what is known, what remains uncertain, and the decision or support you need.

bands.1: A1/A2: meaning is frequently unclear and the task is largely unfulfilled
bands.2: B1: communicates the main message with noticeable limitations
bands.3: B2: communicates clearly and appropriately with generally effective control
bands.4: B2+: handles complexity confidently with only minor lapses
bands.5: C1: precise, flexible, well-structured and consistently effective
